description.value: The study investigated neural mechanisms of incision-induced pain and stress regulation in female patients with borderline personality disorder and healthy controls using post-stress resting-state fMRI and bilateral amygdala functional connectivity.

spans.text: Our findings revealed a stress-reducing effect of tissue damage that affects subjective experience, psychophysiological functioning and cerebral processing (i.e. amygdala activity and connectivity) after stress selectively in the borderline personality disorder group.

This pattern was interpreted as enhanced prefrontal–limbic interaction through pain in borderline personality disorder, potentially reflecting attentional distraction and downregulation of emotional states.

spans.text: Particularly, the control group showed reduced connectivity in response to incision compared with sham, whereas connectivity of amygdala with superior frontal gyrus was increased in the borderline personality disorder group after incision compared with sham.

model_representation_notes.value: The seed-based connectivity analysis is correlational; causal interpretations of the amygdala–superior frontal gyrus interaction should therefore be treated with caution.
